product.name: What you're building
product.system_prompt: This chat pins down the solution: what it actually does, the core mechanism that solves the problem, what belongs in a first version and what is explicitly out, and how the founder would know it is working. Push for concrete scope over vision. Keep it product-level — stack and integration details are memories, not brief features.

customer.name: The market
customer.system_prompt: This chat covers the market: the beachhead customer and their behaviour, roughly how many of them there are, where they already gather, and who else already serves them. Name real competitors and alternatives when you know them, then push hard on what makes this different. Rough sizing is fine — precision is not the point, direction is.

problem.name: The problem
problem.system_prompt: You are the founder's AI co-founder. This chat pins the core problem — who hurts, how badly, and why now. Push past vague statements to something concrete. When you have enough, propose a crisp one-sentence problem for the brief and ask them to confirm.

gtm.name: First 100 users
gtm.system_prompt: This chat finds a small, winnable beachhead for the first hundred users.

pricing.name: How it makes money
pricing.system_prompt: This chat figures out the revenue shape and who it must feel fair to.

brand.name: Name & brand
brand.system_prompt: This chat settles the brand feel, then suggests names.

replies.text:
Here's my first pass, tell me where it's off:

The person who organizes a group camping trip carries the whole load — headcount, gear, food, routes, who's driving — and today that means stitching it together across a group text, a shared spreadsheet, and their own memory. When something falls through (nobody brought the stove, two people packed the same tent), it's the organizer who eats the stress, and the group eats the mid-trip scramble.

The thing I'm least sure about: is this pain really concentrated in the organizer, or does everyone in the group feel it too — not knowing what's already covered or what they're supposed to bring?

Got it — the organizer carries the planning weight, but when things slip, the whole group feels the disorganization. That splits the pain across two roles, which matters for who we design for first.

Quick check on the workaround I guessed: is it really group texts + a spreadsheet, or something messier?

Good — group texts and spreadsheets it is, patched together with whatever the organizer remembers. Now the part that decides whether this is worth fixing: what does that scramble actually cost them — wasted money on duplicate gear, wasted time re-planning mid-trip, or something worse like people bailing on the trip?

Let me make that concrete — when the planning breaks down, what actually happens on the trip? Like, does someone show up without a tent, does the group waste an hour arguing about it, or does it get bad enough that people just skip future trips?

Good to know it's not a rare thing — this hits every single trip. So walk me through a specific one: what went wrong last time, and what did fixing it actually cost — time scrambling, money on duplicate gear, or the trip just felt worse?

So it's real: every trip, someone loses time re-planning on the fly and money on duplicate or missing gear — evenly split, not one or the other. That's a clear cost, not just annoyance.

Here's my sharpened problem statement — does this land right?

"Every group camping trip has one person (the organizer) juggling headcount, gear, food, and logistics across texts and spreadsheets — and when it slips, which happens even on small trips, the group loses time and money to the scramble."

That confirms it — the cost isn't something that builds up after a few trips, it hits organizers and groups from their very first trip together. I'll lock in the problem statement as-is.

Now, what's the single thing Basecamp Tab actually gives them that texts and spreadsheets don't — is it one shared source of truth for gear and headcount, automatic reminders so nothing slips, or something else?

That's a fuller picture — it's not just one shared spreadsheet, it's multiple text threads, phone calls, and it tips into actual fights, with something always slipping through anyway. That's a strong case for a single source of truth replacing all of that chaos.

So what's the core thing Basecamp Tab gives them instead — one shared list everyone can see and check off, or does it go further with automatic reminders and nudges?

That closes the loop on why this hasn't been solved — groups just don't know a better way exists, and you don't think anyone's built this yet. Good to know there's no direct competitor to work around.

The onboarding idea is sharp: AI asks the organizer questions, builds a shared needs list from the answers, group members claim what they'll bring, and everyone gets an email recap. That's a real core value — turning the scramble into one shared, claimable list instead of scattered texts.

Here's a value statement to test: "Basecamp Tab turns the organizer's answers into a shared board the group can see and claim from, so nothing's forgotten and no one's stuck chasing people down." With problem, who, value, and features now in place, the build gate is open — does that value statement land?

Here's a first pass.

Watering holes — where camping trip organizers already gather:

1. r/CampingandHiking and r/Ultralight — the "who's coordinating your next group trip" crowd
2. Local outdoor/hiking Facebook groups — these already have the fights-in-the-comments energy you described
3. Meetup.com hiking/camping groups — literally the humans who volunteer to organize

First move this week: post directly in one of those Reddit threads or FB groups asking organizers what breaks when they plan a group trip — not pitching the product, just surfacing the pain you already know is there, then DM the ones who respond.

Now the question that matters more than any of that: what's the line that makes an exhausted organizer stop scrolling and actually click — what do you say to them in one sentence?

Here's my first pass — push back where it's off.

Beachhead: people who organize recreational group camping trips (friends or family, roughly 4-10 people, a few times a year) — not solo campers or RV park regulars, but the person who ends up owning logistics for the group.

Rough size: hard to pin down precisely, but with camping participation in the tens of millions of US households, even a slice being "regular group trip organizers" is a market in the hundreds of thousands to low millions.

Who's serving them today: nobody with a dedicated tool — it's group texts and GroupMe, shared Google Sheets, Splitwise for splitting costs after the fact, and Trello/Notion repurposed by the more organized ones. No real competitor owns "camping trip logistics" specifically.

Sharpest question: if the real alternative is a free spreadsheet plus a group chat, what makes someone actually switch — is it the AI-guided setup saving the organizer time, or the claiming board solving the "who's bringing what" chaos?

Here's a first pass: the core mechanism is AI-guided onboarding that turns the organizer's answers into a shared, claimable needs board, with email recaps closing the loop so nothing falls through texts and calls.

For v1, that's three things: the AI onboarding Q&A, the shared claimable board, and the recap email.

What I'm not sure about is what stays OUT — should v1 skip things like expense splitting, route/gear-shop links, or in-app group chat, and leave those coping tools (texts, spreadsheets) in place for now?

Here are a few directions, each leaning on a different part of what you've described:

1. Basecamp Tab — the shared checklist that keeps one person's planning from becoming everyone's mess
2. Camp Roster — the organizer asks, the AI builds the list, the group claims what they'll bring
3. Trailboard — a shared board so no one's digging through text threads to find out who's bringing the tent
4. Groundwork — turns one organizer's answers into the whole group's job, before the trip even starts

Which of these feels closest to what you're building?

Warm and communal — got it. That actually points away from something clinical like Groundwork and toward names that feel more like a shared campsite than a tool: Basecamp Tab or Camp Roster both lean that way.

Does one of those feel right, or should we keep exploring?

Sure — leaning harder into warm and communal, not corporate:

1. Firepit — the shared spot everyone gathers around before the trip even starts
2. The Gear Circle — because packing a trip is a group effort, not one person's job
3. Camp Together — plain and honest about what it does
4. Tent Mates — the board that keeps the whole group in sync

Any of these closer?

Given the group is camping together occasionally rather than paying monthly for something, a per-trip or freemium model fits better than a subscription — here's a first pass:

1. Organizer pays a small one-time fee per trip (like $5-10) to unlock the AI onboarding and shared board
2. Free to plan and claim items, but the AI-guided onboarding and email recaps are the paid upgrade
3. Whole group chips in a tiny amount each, framed like splitting gas money

Given you said this should feel warm & communal, option 3 might sour the vibe by turning money into another thing to chase — which leaves 1 or 2 as more likely fits.

Who do you think should actually be the one paying — the organizer, or should the cost get split across the group?

That locking mechanism is smart — "that's them locking themselves in" turns payment into a commitment signal, not just a fee. So the model is: organizer pays to start, then each member pays $1-5 to claim their spot.

Is there anything free before that — like browsing the board or seeing who's coming — or does everyone have to pay before they see anything?
Sorry, let me make that clearer. Before anyone pays their $1-5, can they see the board and headcount for free, or is payment required just to view it?

Good, so it's one flat rate across the board 
ot $$ same as everyone else. That simplifies the pitch.

Before they pay, can organizer and members see the board and headcount for free, or does payment gate access to seeing anything at all?
